product_target.statement: Moria is a reusable Rust voxel-world substrate consumed through public crate interfaces by games and a minimal non-game validation executable; this repository delivers the substrate and its public-API validation commitments, not any particular game or the later Product One explorer demo.

documents.rationale: Repository overview that points at the mixed-project brief as the product definition and labels the interface note as supporting context; its editorial framing is evidence, not self-authenticating authority.

States the current product boundary, capabilities, public API, validation commitments, non-goals, and explicitly marks embedded Product One paragraphs as future-consumer context that does not authorize game content in Moria.
Describes the reusable consumer-facing surface that supports the program brief and states that it does not add deliverables.

claims.statement: Moria is the reusable voxel-world substrate defined by docs/seeds/mixed-project-brief.md; only the current substrate commitments are deliverables in this repository, and the substrate interface reference supplies supporting technical context without expanding product scope.

Moria is a reusable Rust voxel-world substrate consumed through public crate interfaces by games and by a minimal validation executable; this repository delivers the substrate, not any particular game.

The current product owns deterministic seed-based generation, sparse voxel storage, bounded streaming, mutation, surface extraction, persistence, and read-only diagnostics that must remain useful to multiple downstream consumers.

External consumers can create and identify a world, request bounded regions, observe readiness, query material truth, submit bounded edits, and persist deltas, and must not reach into storage, meshing, or scheduler internals.

The validation executable uses exactly the public interfaces, may provide a free-fly camera and diagnostics sufficient to exercise the crate, is not a game prototype, and owns no privileged world path.
Generation is deterministic for the same versioned parameters and seed.

Mutation is admitted through a bounded command API and committed atomically; persistence restores the same authoritative material state; derived meshes and diagnostics never become authoritative world state.

Streaming must bound resident work and expose observable lifecycle states; background results carry generation identities so stale work cannot replace newer truth; failures remain typed and observable to public consumers.

Headless fixtures cover generation, query, mutation, persistence, and lifecycle behavior; a small visual fixture demonstrates that a relocated external consumer can render and edit through the public API; performance is reported with machine identity and this brief does not establish a machine-specific correctness threshold.

Moria does not implement game rules, combat, inventory, AI, narrative systems, characters, animation, authored levels, or production content; references to possible consumers explain interface pressure only.

After the reusable substrate ships, a separate Product One repository may place a third-person explorer in a generated region with hills, a dense mixed forest, a river, and a cave, and that later game-facing demo may use skeletal animation and a curated cliff-to-cave traversal to communicate the world.

A later Product One game-facing demo may include a dense mixed forest in a generated region, but that forest population workload is future-consumer context and is not authorized as a Moria deliverable.

The later-consumer paragraphs embedded in this binding program brief do not authorize a player controller, character mesh, animation clips, forest population workload, curated route, or game asset in Moria.
The substrate interface reference supports the Moria program brief, describes the reusable surface downstream consumers need, and does not add deliverables.

The reusable surface includes world identity from format version, generation parameters, and seed; readiness and bounded material queries; bounded mutation commands with admission failures and commit revisions; streaming lifecycle states; authoritative-delta persistence; registered objects that are not game entities; and diagnostics without mutable internal handles.
